name: HIAS: programmes for refugees abroad
beneficiaries_note: Our build: HIAS's country programmes weighted by our judgment of where the spending and the result go, as HIAS publishes no spending by country: Chad (257,700 served, many through cheap camp-wide services, and most of the cash), then Colombia, Ecuador and Panama (36,700, about 21,000 and 23,000 served, with more cash per person and the legal work), Ukraine and Moldova (32,300), Costa Rica, Mexico, Venezuela, Kenya, Israel, Greece and the Resettlement Support Center in Austria (Form 990 Schedule O).
summary: HIAS spent $48.1 million in the year to September 2025 on programmes for refugees and displaced people in about 15 countries, the largest for Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad and for Venezuelans and others across Latin America: cash and basic needs for 54,000 people (33,000 in Chad), legal protection for 81,000, violence prevention and support for 80,500, mental-health support for 73,100, child protection for 127,000 children and economic inclusion for 6,000 (calendar 2025 counts), and the US Resettlement Support Center in Austria until admissions stopped. Each activity is built from the research on that kind of work: cash and goods on the site's log-income scale (with a few crisis deaths averted in Chad's camps), legal status from Colombia's regularisation natural experiment, mental-health, survivors' and children's support in life satisfaction from humanitarian trials, economic inclusion from the graduation trials, and the refugees processed for the US by the consumption they gain there. It comes to about 0.05 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.01-0.2), because much of the spending is on protection and legal work whose measurable gains are small per person; cash in Chad gives over half of it. Every branch is discounted for missing data: HIAS counts the people reached but publishes no controlled measure of its own results; the biggest uncertainties are that discount, displaced people's consumption and the share of the payments that reaches people as cash.

Donated legal services, booked in the accounts at the law firms' rates, are not HIAS's own money: they enter the credit share, not the cost.

sections.explainer: How many people the spending reached, as HIAS reports it.

sections.title: Effect per person
sections.explainer: What the help does for each person reached, from the research on that kind of work, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, delivery falling short and missing outcome data. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction) and put into healthy years by its unit's conversion, so each moves only with its own sliders.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in healthy years, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Refugees processed by the Resettlement Support Center in Austria who left for the US in the year
rows.explainer: A judgment: HIAS publishes no count and we found no published departures from Austria. Basis: HIAS ran the State Department's Resettlement Support Center in Vienna (statements note 1: the grants 'expired' on 31 December 2025; a director on the Form 990's Part VII), whose caseload is mainly Iranian religious minorities under the Lautenberg programme. 278 Iranian Christians were resettled in fiscal 2024 (Article Eighteen, https://articleeighteen.com/?p=15233), and Jews, Baháʼís and others add to them (about 700 Iranian Jews were left waiting by the 2025 ban: J. The Jewish News of Northern California, 6 March 2025): roughly 500 a year. Departures stopped with the January 2025 suspension, so only October 2024 to January 2025 counts, four months: about 200 (50 if few travelled before the suspension, 600 if departures were bunched before it). 200 (50-600).

rows.explainer: The counts are for calendar 2025, but the cost is October 2024 to September 2025, whose first quarter ran at the higher pre-cut level (20 countries, spending $80 million a year before against $48 million for the year: Exhibit B). 1.15 (1-1.3). Our judgment.

rows.label: Death rate of the cash recipients in Chad (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad's camps, where surveys since 2023 found crude death rates near or above the emergency threshold of 1 per 10,000 a day (3.65% a year): 2% a year (1.2-3.5%). Our judgment. The Latin American recipients are counted at no excess death.

rows.label: Normal death rate (per person-year)
rows.explainer: The site's Sudan figure (UN World Population Prospects), the rate the refugees would face at home in peace.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths averted for the people reached
rows.explainer: Cash and food lower crisis mortality modestly where people go hungry; transfers are small next to the camps' needs. 3% (0-10%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years of the crisis the help covers
rows.explainer: One to six months of transfers. A quarter of a year (0.1-0.5). Our judgment.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person given cash and basic needs
rows.explainer: Only the Chad recipients, at the camps' excess death rate.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted under five

rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person given cash and basic needs (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Clean water (4,200 people in Venezuela) and food avert some diarrhoea and malnutrition: a small amount. Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of conflict-affected people with a mental disorder

source.title: Charlson et al. (2019), New WHO prevalence estimates of mental disorders in conflict settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis, The Lancet 394:240-248
source.quote: The mean prevalence of mental disorders (depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia) was 22.1% (95% UI 18.8-25.7) at any point in time in the conflict-affected populations assessed.

rows.explainer: The share of a general displaced population with a disorder: used for the violence and child-protection branches, whose participants aren't screened.

rows.label: Share of the mental-health count given structured support (counselling, groups)
rows.explainer: The count includes people reached through awareness sessions and trained community members; HIAS served 13,000 in Chad with services and over 900 in Kenya directly (Form 990 Schedule O). 30% (15-50%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of those in structured support with significant distress
rows.explainer: The same rule as the other branches (the effect counts only for people with distress), but people referred to counselling and groups are screened or self-select for distress, far above the 22% of a general displaced population (Charlson et al. 2019). 60% (40-80%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Effect of the support on distress, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: WHO's low-intensity psychological interventions for people exposed to adversity reduce distress by 0.45 SD (0.34-0.56) across 23 trials (Schäfer et al. 2023, World Psychiatry, https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.21129); HIAS's community-based psychosocial support is less structured than the trials' programmes: 0.3 SD (0.15-0.5). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the effect lasts
rows.explainer: Follow-ups of brief psychological interventions show effects fading over one to two years: a year at full effect (0.5-2), as in the site's other humanitarian models. Our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person counted, discounted
rows.explainer: SD-years × the site's WELLBYs per SD-year, for the distressed people in structured support, over the whole count.

rows.label: Share of the violence count given direct support (case management, safe spaces, survivors' care)
rows.explainer: The rest attend awareness sessions or community trainings. 40% (20-60%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Effect of survivors' care and protection on distress, in SDs, for those with a disorder
rows.explainer: Psychosocial support and case management for survivors reduce distress by small to moderate amounts in humanitarian trials; the same 0.3 SD (0.1-0.5) as the site's Save the Children protection branch. Our judgment.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per directly supported person from less violence (points a year)
rows.explainer: Community prevention programmes cut intimate partner violence in some trials (SASA! in Uganda by about half: Abramsky et al. 2014), less often in camps; a small fall in risk spread over all participants: 0.05 points (0-0.2). Our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person counted, discounted
rows.explainer: Distress relieved for those with a disorder and less violence for all directly supported, over the same years as mental-health support.

rows.label: Share of the children given direct services (case management, child-friendly spaces, groups)
rows.explainer: The rest are reached by awareness campaigns, as for the mental-health and violence branches' indirect reach. 60% (30-90%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of the children not already counted in another branch's benefit
rows.explainer: Many of the children are in families given cash or in the violence programmes; the youth-tailored count overlaps them. 50% (30-80%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Effect of child protection and psychosocial support on children's distress, in SDs, for those with a disorder
rows.explainer: Focused psychosocial support for children in humanitarian settings lowers post-traumatic stress by 0.33 SD (95% CI 0.14-0.52) in an individual-participant meta-analysis of 11 trials, less for displaced children (Purgato et al. 2018, Lancet Global Health 6:e390, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(18)30046-9); HIAS's child-friendly spaces and case management are less structured. 0.2 SD (0.05-0.4). Our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs per child counted, discounted
rows.formula: cp_direct_share * cp_new_share * share_distressed * cp_effect_sd * @wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, mh_effect_years)

rows.label: Share of the legal count given individual assistance or representation
rows.explainer: The rest get legal information sessions. 35% (20-60%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Extra chance the help wins a person legal status or documents
rows.explainer: Regularisation drives such as Colombia's PEP and Temporary Protection Status are open to many who don't know how to apply or can't prove eligibility; legal aid helps some of them through. 10% (3-25%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Consumption gain from legal status (share)

source.title: Ibáñez, Moya, Ortega, Rozo and Urbina (2024), Life Out of the Shadows: Impacts of Amnesties in the Lives of Refugees (Joint Data Center literature review)
source.quote: Specifically, PEP led to a 48 percent increase in per capita consumption, a 22 percent increase in labor income

rows.explainer: Venezuelan migrants in Colombia granted the PEP permit against those who arrived just after the cut-off: a credible natural experiment, in the place where HIAS does much of its legal work. The published version's 48%; an earlier working paper reported 60% (IZA DP 15049), and the mechanisms (transfers, bank accounts) reach only part of those eligible: 48% (30-60%).

rows.label: Share of the legal count in Latin America
rows.explainer: Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador and Mexico hold most of HIAS's legal work; Chad, Kenya, Israel and Europe the rest. 60% (40-80%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Status gain elsewhere, as a share of Colombia's
rows.explainer: In Chad's camps and Kenya, papers bring fewer jobs and services than a work permit in Colombia; in Israel and Europe status protects against deportation. Half (20-80%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the status gain lasts
rows.explainer: Permits run two to ten years; some would regularise later without help. 3 years (1-6). Our judgment.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person in the legal count
rows.formula: leg_direct_share * leg_status_uplift * ln(1 + status_consumption_gain) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, status_years) * (leg_lac_share + (1 - leg_lac_share) * leg_other_ratio)

rows.label: Household consumption gain from the graduation programme, a year (share)
rows.explainer: The graduation approach raised consumption by about 5-10% three years on in six countries (Banerjee et al. 2015, Science, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1260799); refugee versions, like HIAS's in Ecuador, add job placement and seed capital with mixed results. 6% (2-15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Gain of the other economic participants, as a share of the graduation gain
rows.explainer: The other 4,900 get workshops, job referrals or small seed grants (about $13 a family for some), much lighter than graduation. A quarter (10-50%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years the consumption gain lasts
rows.explainer: Graduation gains held at seven to ten years in Bangladesh and India; refugees move more. 3 years (1-7). Our judgment.

rows.label: People in a participant's household
rows.explainer: The site's household size for Peru, standing in for Ecuador and Colombia.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per participant's household, discounted
rows.formula: (eco_grad_people / eco_people + (1 - eco_grad_people / eco_people) * eco_light_ratio) * ln(1 + eco_consumption_gain) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, eco_years) * eco_household_size
rows.explainer: Every member of the participant's household consumes more; graduation participants at the full gain, the rest at the lighter one.

rows.label: Resettled refugees' consumption in the US (US$)
Resettled refugees' consumption, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: As in the site's HIAS advocacy model: near the poorest fifth's level over their years, 40% (30-55%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Consumption per person, Egypt (PPP dollars, 2024)
rows.explainer: The site's household-survey consumption per person (World Bank PIP mean, 2021 PPP dollars a day, × 365, US prices to 2024, real growth to 2024), in purchasing-power dollars, so it compares directly with US consumption.

rows.label: Consumption where the refugees come from (PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: Egypt stands in for Iran, which the site has no survey figure for (a judgment; Iran's consumption is similar or higher, so the gain may be overstated).

rows.label: Years in the US gained per refugee
rows.explainer: The Lautenberg programme's refugees are families of all ages: 30 years (15-45). Our judgment.

cva: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Cash and goods counted at their value; vouchers and in-kind goods are worth a little less to people than cash. 0.85 (0.7-1), as in the site's other relief models. Our judgment.

rows.explainer: Other agencies (UNHCR, WFP, the Red Cross) give cash in the same places, more so before the 2025 cuts. 70% (45-90%). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: The trials' effects come from structured programmes with trained facilitators; community-based delivery and the step from distress scales to life satisfaction add doubt. 0.6 (0.4-0.9), as for the site's Save the Children protection branch. Our judgment.

rows.explainer: The effect is against trials' control arms; few other services exist in eastern Chad's camps. 90% (80-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: mh: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Partners and UNHCR co-fund some sites. 85% (70-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: mh: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.explainer: The effects are from trials of other programmes, the prevention evidence mixed in camps. 0.55 (0.3-0.85). Our judgment.

rows.label: gbv: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Other protection agencies cover some of the same camps and towns. 85% (70-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: gbv: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: UNHCR and UNFPA co-fund and coordinate. 80% (60-95%). Our judgment.

rows.label: gbv: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: cp: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Children's psychosocial trials show small, inconsistent effects, and a distress-to-life-satisfaction step made for adults. 0.5 (0.3-0.8). Our judgment.

rows.label: cp: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: UNICEF and other child-protection agencies work in the same camps. 85% (70-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: cp: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: UNHCR and UNICEF co-fund child protection in the camps and towns where HIAS works, and community volunteers run some child-friendly spaces: HIAS's share 80% (60-95%), as for its other protection work. Our judgment.

rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): HIAS counts the people reached, but publishes no controlled measure of what its own work did for them; the effect is from research on other programmes, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: leg: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The consumption gain is from a credible natural experiment, but the share of clients whose status changes because of HIAS is a judgment. 0.65 (0.4-0.9). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: The graduation trials' effects transfer only partly to urban refugees. 0.65 (0.4-0.9). Our judgment.

rows.label: eco: share that wouldn't have happened anyway

rows.label: rsc: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The gain is the consumption gap and the years, judged from survey figures with a stand-in country. 0.7 (0.5-0.9). Our judgment.

rows.label: rsc: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Reference class: the State Department re-awards Resettlement Support Centers to other operators (the IOM, other NGOs) when one stops; without HIAS another would have processed the same cases, a little later. 15% (5-35%). Our judgment.

rows.label: rsc: HIAS's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Admission is the US government's decision; the IOM moves the refugees and a US agency resettles them: HIAS's processing is one of several resources. 30% (15-50%). Our judgment.

rows.label: rsc: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): the departures are our judgment (HIAS publishes no count) and the gain is judged from survey figures, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: HIAS's counts are its own and some people counted get only a session or a single transfer; programmes were cut mid-year. 0.9 (0.75-1). The calendar-year counts' gap to the fiscal year is in reach_period_adj. Our judgment.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: After the 2025 cuts few funders fill the gaps a donation fills. 1 (0.9-1.05). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: HIAS ended the year with $4.4 million of cash against $153 million of spending (Exhibit A): money is spent within weeks. 0.15 (0.05-0.4). Our judgment.
